title: What are network effects, and how do you handle a platform case?
description: Why platforms like marketplaces and social networks behave differently, what network effects are, and how to structure a platform case.
hook: Some of the most common case topics today involve platforms: delivery apps, ride-hailing, marketplaces, payment apps. They behave differently from ordinary businesses, and if you use a standard framework without adjusting, you can miss the point. The key idea to understand is the network effect.
body:
What a network effect is

A product has a network effect when it becomes more valuable as more people use it. One phone is useless; a phone network everyone uses is invaluable. Social networks, messaging apps and marketplaces all work this way.

Two-sided platforms

Many platforms have two groups of users who need each other: riders and drivers, diners and restaurants, buyers and sellers. More drivers mean shorter waits, which attracts more riders, which attracts more drivers. This loop is powerful once it starts, but hard to start. That is called the chicken-and-egg problem.

What this means in a case

  • Always look at both sides. A drop in orders on a delivery app might be a restaurant problem (fewer good restaurants) rather than a customer problem.
  • Think local. A ride-hailing app's network effect is mostly within a city. Being big in London does not help much in Leeds.
  • Subsidies make sense early. Paying drivers bonuses or giving customers discounts can be rational to start the loop, but should shrink as the network grows.
  • Watch the take rate. The platform's cut has to be low enough that both sides stay, and high enough to make money.

A structure for "Should we launch our platform in a new city?"

  • Demand side: how many potential customers, how often they would use it
  • Supply side: how many drivers, restaurants or sellers we can sign up, and at what cost
  • Getting to critical mass: subsidies needed and for how long
  • Competition: is there already a strong local platform?
  • Unit economics once mature: profit per order or trip

A worked example: the take rate

A ride costs a passenger £20 and the platform keeps 25%, so £5. If it pays drivers a £2 bonus per trip to attract them in a new city, it keeps only £3. If insurance, payments and support cost £2.50 a trip, the platform earns 50p. Once the city has enough drivers, the bonus can fall and each trip earns £2.50. That is why platforms accept losses early.
